subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which piece of apparatus is designed to deliver a fixed, accurate volume such as 25.0 cm3 of solution in a titration?
questions.explain: A pipette is calibrated to deliver a single fixed volume very accurately, unlike a beaker or measuring cylinder.

questions.q: How does the melting point of a pure solid differ from that of an impure sample?
options: A pure solid melts sharply at a specific temperature
A pure solid melts over a wide range of temperatures
A pure solid has no fixed melting point
A pure solid always melts at a lower temperature than an impure one
questions.explain: Purity is shown by a sharp, fixed melting point, whereas impurities cause melting over a range.

questions.q: What effect does an impurity have on the melting point of a solid substance?
options: It lowers the melting point and makes melting occur over a range
It raises the melting point to a single sharp value
It has no effect on the melting point
It removes the melting point entirely
questions.explain: Impurities lower the melting point and broaden it into a range rather than a sharp point.

questions.q: A student wants to measure the volume of carbon dioxide gas produced during a reaction over time. Which apparatus is most suitable?
questions.explain: A gas syringe collects and measures the volume of gas released as the reaction proceeds.

questions.q: Which technique is used to separate an insoluble solid from a liquid?
questions.explain: Filtration traps the insoluble solid (residue) while the liquid (filtrate) passes through the filter paper.

questions.q: Why is crystallisation, rather than simple evaporation to dryness, used to obtain pure crystals of a soluble salt from its solution?
options: It avoids decomposing the salt and allows large, pure crystals to form
It removes an insoluble solid from the mixture
It measures the boiling point of the solvent
questions.explain: Slow crystallisation from a saturated solution gives pure, well-formed crystals without heating the salt to dryness where it might decompose.

questions.q: Which property allows fractional distillation to separate a mixture of ethanol and water?
options: One is soluble and one is insoluble
They have different densities and are immiscible
questions.explain: Fractional distillation separates miscible liquids because they boil at different temperatures, with the lower-boiling ethanol distilling first.

questions.q: Which method would you use to obtain pure water from a sample of seawater?
questions.explain: The water is boiled off and condensed as pure liquid, leaving the dissolved salts behind.

questions.q: A student needs to separate a mixture of oil and water, which do not mix. Which apparatus should be used?
questions.explain: Immiscible liquids form two layers, so the lower layer can be run off through the tap of a separating funnel.

questions.q: What is the test result that confirms a gas is hydrogen?
options: It gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint
questions.explain: Hydrogen burns explosively in a small test, producing the characteristic squeaky pop.

questions.q: Which gas relights a glowing splint?
questions.explain: Oxygen supports combustion, so it relights a glowing splint.

questions.q: Which gas turns limewater milky (cloudy)?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide reacts with limewater to form insoluble calcium carbonate, turning it milky.

questions.q: A pungent gas turns damp red litmus paper blue. Which gas is it?
questions.explain: Ammonia is alkaline, so it turns damp red litmus paper blue.

questions.q: Which gas bleaches damp litmus paper?
questions.explain: Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper, turning it white.

questions.q: Adding sodium hydroxide solution to a solution produces a light blue precipitate that is insoluble in excess. Which ion is present?
questions.explain: Cu2+ ions form a light blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide with sodium hydroxide.

questions.q: A solution gives a red-brown precipitate when sodium hydroxide solution is added. Which cation does it contain?
questions.explain: Fe3+ ions form a red-brown precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide with sodium hydroxide.

questions.q: Dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate solution is added to an unknown solution, giving a cream precipitate. Which ion is present?
questions.explain: Bromide ions give a cream precipitate of silver bromide, whereas chloride gives white and iodide gives yellow.

questions.q: What is added, after acidifying with dilute nitric acid, to test for the presence of a sulfate ion?
options: Barium nitrate solution, giving a white precipitate
Silver nitrate solution, giving a yellow precipitate
Sodium hydroxide, giving a blue precipitate
questions.explain: Sulfate ions form a white precipitate of barium sulfate with acidified barium nitrate solution.

questions.q: Which expression correctly gives the Rf value of a spot in chromatography?
options: distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent
distance moved by solvent / distance moved by substance
distance moved by substance x distance moved by solvent
distance moved by solvent - distance moved by substance
questions.explain: The Rf value equals the distance travelled by the substance divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front.

questions.q: Why is the baseline on a chromatogram drawn in pencil rather than ink?
options: Pencil does not dissolve and move up with the solvent
Pencil is easier to see than ink
Ink reacts chemically with the paper
Pencil makes the spots travel faster
questions.explain: Pencil is insoluble in the solvent, so it stays put, whereas ink would dissolve and travel up the paper.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry (0620) syllabus; Experimental Techniques & Analysis
